\section[ignōsce mihi]{ignōsce mihi — "forgive me" / I'm sorry}

\label{lesson:LA-C04-ignosce-mihi}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You've met \textbf{quaesō}, the worn-down "I ask" Romans used for \emph{please}. Their word for \emph{sorry} is built the very same way — a small verb carrying the whole apology.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{ignōsce} — the imperative "\textbf{forgive!}," from \textbf{ignōscere}, itself \textbf{in-} (here appearing as \textbf{ig-}, "not") + \textbf{(g)nōscere}, "\textbf{to know.}" Literally, \emph{ignōscere} means "\textbf{to not-know}" — i.e. to overlook, to treat as unseen. Asking forgiveness in Latin is asking someone \emph{not to hold something against you}, as if they hadn't noticed it.
  \item \textbf{mihi} — "\textbf{to me}," the dative pronoun.
\end{itemize}

So \textbf{ignōsce mihi} is "\textbf{forgive {[}it{]} to me}" — \emph{don't hold this against me.}

That root \textbf{(g)nōscere}, "to know," reaches deep into English: \textbf{know} itself traces to the very same ancient root, alongside \textbf{recognize} ("know again"), \textbf{cognition}, and \textbf{notice}. Latin's word for "sorry" and English's word for "know" are, at bottom, blood relatives.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Latin also had an \textbf{impersonal} construction for plain regret — no imperative, no "you" at all: \textbf{paenitet mē}, literally "\textbf{it grieves me}" (\emph{mē} here is accusative, "me," the one afflicted by the regret) — \emph{"I regret {[}it{]}."} It comes from the verb \textbf{paenitēre}, "to cause regret," the direct ancestor of English \textbf{penitent}, \textbf{penitence}, and \textbf{repent}.

Where \textbf{ignōsce mihi} asks someone to \textbf{forgive} you, \textbf{paenitet mē} simply names your own \textbf{regret} — closer to "I'm sorry {[}that happened{]}" than to "please forgive me." The same regret/forgiveness split you'll meet again and again across languages.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "ignōsce" — forgive — then "mihi," to me{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the whole phrase — "ignōsce mihi" = forgive me{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the other one — "paenitet mē" = I regret it{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{ignōsce mihi} literally mean, piece by piece? (\textbf{"Forgive to me"} — \emph{ignōscere} "to not-know/overlook" + \emph{mihi} "to me.") What English words share the \emph{(g)nōscere} root? (\textbf{Know, recognize, cognition, notice}.) What's Latin's other way to express regret, and how is it different? (\textbf{Paenitet mē}, "it grieves me" — names the regret, rather than asking to be forgiven.)
\end{tcolorbox}
